options: The flow of electric charge along a path
questions.explanation: Current is charge in motion — the electrons marching through the wire.
questions.misconception: Voltage (the push) and current (the flow) are often swapped.

questions.prompt: In what unit is electric current measured?
questions.explanation: Amps measure the rate of charge flow; volts measure the push, ohms the resistance.
questions.misconception: Volt (push), ohm (resistance), and amp (flow) get mixed up on appliance labels.

questions.prompt: You cut one wire of a lamp circuit. What happens to the current?
options: It doubles on the other side
questions.explanation: Current needs a complete loop; a single break anywhere stops the whole circuit.
questions.misconception: Thinking current still reaches parts beyond the cut; a series loop is all-or-nothing.

questions.prompt: You increase the current through a bulb. What do you expect?
questions.explanation: More charge passing the filament each second means more energy each second — brighter light.
questions.misconception: The direction of the current/brightness link is sometimes flipped.

questions.prompt: In one simple loop, the current near the battery compared with near the bulb is...
questions.explanation: A series loop carries one shared current; it cannot pile up or empty in one spot.
questions.misconception: Thinking current 'spends itself' along the wire; it flows as one equal flow everywhere.
